messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran is a 74-year-old software engineer who came to treatment after months of worsening sleep, saying she felt as if her body had never really left the hospital where her daughter nearly died. Although the medical crisis happened years ago, she still speaks about it in the present tense at times, as if the danger might resume the moment she stops paying attention. Her daughter had developed a sudden life-threatening illness and was rushed into intensive care. Linh remembers long stretches of waiting beside machines and doors that did not open quickly enough, the sharp antiseptic smell on her clothes and hands, and the terrible moments when the usual hospital noise dropped away. What lodged in her most deeply was not only the fear, but the silence before staff came in, the kind of silence that felt unnatural, suspended, as though it announced catastrophe. She had driven back and forth to the hospital for days, and even now the sound of passing cars can pull her straight back to those urgent drives when she believed she might be arriving too late.

In the months after her daughter recovered, Linh found that certain moments reached her before she had time to think. If a room fell suddenly quiet, or she caught the smell of disinfectant in a clinic, office hallway, or even on someone’s freshly cleaned hands, she was hit by the same terror she had felt while waiting for news. At times there was no picture in her mind at all, only a wave of dread and bodily certainty that something awful was already happening. Car sounds could do the same thing, especially when she was working from home and heard tires passing outside in the evening; she would feel her chest tighten as if she were once again on the road to the hospital. These moments did not stay as mere reminders. In the same instant, she would think, with renewed conviction, that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that disaster can arrive without warning. The triggers seemed to prove to her that safety is an illusion.

As these episodes continued, Linh became increasingly sure that she had failed in some essential way during her daughter’s illness. When the memories came back with full force, shame accompanied them. She would replay decisions she made, conversations she had with doctors, the timing of when she left or returned, and she had come to believe that the event happened because of the way she acted, or because she had not acted quickly or correctly enough. The terror of remembering and the shame of remembering fused into a broader conclusion: bad things happen, and when they do, she cannot stop them. That sense of helplessness hardened over time into a worldview in which danger is always near and she is never truly capable of preventing it.

That belief has shaped her days and especially her nights. Linh says she has difficulty falling asleep because some part of her feels she needs to stay alert. If she lets herself settle into the quiet of the house, the silence feels loaded, like the charged stillness outside an ICU room, and she becomes superalert, listening for sounds in the street or elsewhere in the home. Because she sees the world as dangerous and herself as unable to stop what is coming, staying watchful feels necessary rather than excessive. Her vigilance has spread into ordinary settings. At work, even though she remains highly competent, she notices car sounds outside the office or sudden lulls in open-plan noise and immediately scans for what might be wrong. She has begun keeping background audio on while coding because complete silence feels intolerable.

The more on guard Linh stays, the more easily she detects the very cues that undo her. A brief hush in a meeting, the antiseptic scent in a medical building near her workplace, or traffic outside her window catches her attention instantly because she is already listening and searching. That sharpened watchfulness makes the triggers feel omnipresent, and once noticed, they bring back the terror again—sometimes vividly, sometimes as raw emotion without a clear scene attached. After nights of lying awake in a state of alert anticipation, the memories are even closer to the surface the next day, and she finds herself once more pulled into shame and self-blame about what happened to her daughter.

Linh finally sought help when her husband told her that the house no longer felt restful because she could not tolerate quiet and rarely slept through the night. She was distressed by how small her world was becoming around sounds, smells, and vigilance she could not switch off. What frightens her most is the sense that if she ever stops monitoring, another catastrophe will strike and she will again be powerless to prevent it. What she hopes, cautiously, is not to erase what happened to her daughter, but to live in a world that no longer feels moments away from disaster.
